As of 425 AM Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... A Heat Advisory has been issued for this afternoon 
for Cumberland, Hoke, Sampson, Scotland, and Wayne Co., for the risk 
of 2-3 hours of heat index values to around 105 F. 

Near persistence heat and humidity, which yielded heat index values 
of 100-107 F over parts of the Sandhills and Coastal Plain on 
Monday, will probably do the same this afternoon. Sea breeze 
convection and outflow in the srn and cntl Coastal Plain will have 
the potential to shorten the duration of advisory criteria heat, or 
prevent it altogether.
 

KEY MESSAGE 2... After a scattering of afternoon sea breeze and 
possibly Piedmont trough convection today, showers/storms will 
increase in coverage across the nrn Piedmont later tonight into Wed, 
then settle, with an associated outflow-reinforced frontal zone, 
sewd and across most all of cntl NC through Wed night.

A series of vigorous shortwave perturbations will amplify an 
anomalously deep synoptic trough, with standardized 500 mb height 
anomalies forecast to reach 2-3 sigma, across the Great Lakes and 
middle Atlantic through mid-week. In a tight height gradient at its 
base, the mid-latitude westerlies will dip to atypically low 
latitudes for this time of year, with 500-700 mb winds of 30-50 kts 
likely from the Virginias to nrn NC from late this afternoon through 
Wed, atop a broad region of lwr-level warm air advection and 
contribution to QG forcing for ascent.

At the surface, an outflow-reinforced front will progress across the 
lwr OH Valley and Virginias through early tonight, then settle 
across srn VA and possibly into the nrn Piedmont and nrn Coastal 
Plain of NC late tonight-early Wed. It will be preceded by a pre-
frontal, Appalachian-lee trough over the srn Middle Atlantic 
Piedmont today. The front will then waver over cntl NC Wed-Wed 
night, modulated by training convection/outflow and differential 
diabatic heating, and probably settle into SC and sern NC by early 
Thu.

Afternoon showers/storms today will likely concentrate in the srn 
and cntl Coastal Plain and possibly the nw Piedmont, along the sea 
breeze and Piedmont trough, respectively. While the most intense 
cells will be capable of producing damaging downburst winds, the 
aforementioned strengthening mid-level winds across nrn NC will 
conditionally favor multi-cell clustering along common cold pools 
and a somewhat greater risk of damaging wind gusts, where a Slight 
risk for severe storms, Level 2 of 5, remains.

Training and backbuilding convection, with an increasing risk of 
excessive rain and flash flooding, will then become favored along 
the outflow-reinforced frontal zone over srn VA and nrn NC late 
tonight-early Wed, before settling swd across most of all cntl NC 
later Wed-Wed night. A categorical upgrade from Slight risk to 
Moderate for excessive rain may become necessary (Level 2 to 3) as 
uncertainties from mesoscale and convective influences to the 
placement and evolution of the boundary become clearer; and a Flash 
Flood Watch may be needed by later this afternoon or overnight. 
While a few strong to severe downbursts will also be possible, the 
flash flood risk will have become relatively greater by Wed. 


KEY MESSAGE 3... A cold front will move across NC on Thursday and 
then stall across the Carolinas into the weekend producing a period 
of unsettled weather with cooler than average temperatures. There is 
significant uncertainty in the placement of the front which will 
greatly determine forecast details including the potential for 
significant rainfall. 

A mid and upper-level trough will persist across the Great Lakes and 
Northeast through the Thursday through Monday period. A cold front 
will move south across NC on Thursday and likely stall across along 
the Carolina coast and extend westward somewhere in the Carolinas on 
Friday through Monday. The front will mark the leading edge of a 
cooler and more stable airmass and the frontal zone will be the 
focus for showers and thunderstorms through much of the period. 

While the operational GFS and EC move the front into NC on Thursday 
night and then waver it near the NC/SC border or even across eastern 
NC on Friday through the weekend the various GEFS and ENS ensemble 
members provide a wide range of solutions including pushing the 
front further south through SC into GA while others lift the front 
across NC into VA. Climatology would suggest a significant southward 
push would be unusual and a northward retreat would be more common. 
In addition sub-synoptic factors including the development of 
convection near the front could impact the evolution and placement 
of the front. 

Notably cooler and drier air will setup behind the front with much 
lower precipitation chances. Near the frontal zone and especially 
south of the front expect much more cloudiness, muggy conditions and 
unsettled weather with multiple rounds of showers and storms. On
